lines.text: Do you know how the northern lights work? Those glowing curtains in the sky actually start ninety three million miles away, at the Sun.
The Sun is always throwing off a stream of charged particles, called the solar wind. It reaches Earth in about two to four days.
Earth has a shield. Its magnetic field steers most of those particles around the planet.
But near the poles, the field lines dive down into the atmosphere, and some particles slide down them.
About a hundred kilometers up, they slam into oxygen and nitrogen in the air. That gives those atoms extra energy, and they release it as light.
Oxygen glows green, and higher up, red. Nitrogen adds blue and purple at the edges.
From space, the lights form a ring around each pole. In the south, they're called the southern lights.
When the Sun throws out a huge burst, called a coronal mass ejection, the ring grows, and people see auroras far from the poles.
So every aurora is the Sun, painting our sky.
